title: Orchid Labs Integration Eval — proxy-first SDK & LangChain flow
topics: Rate limits, quotas, and token accounting
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private TCO
summary: Discovery call focused on how Orchid Labs would integrate Redwood behind a proxy-first architecture. Customer is evaluating hosted for fast experiment, dedicated for production throughput, and private for data residency. Key concerns: gateway sidecar pattern, per-route quotas, KV cache behavior with LangChain agents, and observability/tracing hooks for SLOs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03 15:00 UTC | Duration: 47m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE); Liam O'Connor (CTO, Orchid), Priya Desai (ML Eng), Marco Ruiz (SRE), Evelyn Park (Product)

[00:00] Jordan Patel: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time today, um we wanted to run through how folks at Orchid are thinking about integrating Redwood, specifically since you mentioned a proxy-led architecture in the email.

[00:18] Liam O'Connor: yeah thanks Jordan. quick context — we're prototyping an agent platform on top of LangChain and LlamaIndex, most traffic is internal but we have to support partner-facing endpoints eventually. main ask is: can Redwood sit behind our gateway without losing observability or token accounting?

[00:38] Maya Chen: totally. high level, Redwood supports a few integration patterns — direct SDK calls from backend, a proxy/gateway in front of the API, or sidecar per service. each has tradeoffs around latency, batching, and quotas.

[00:55] Priya Desai: can you expand on the proxy pattern? we currently use an envoy-based gateway. we want rate limits per organization + per-route quotas and also want to tie usage back to billing.

[01:12] Maya Chen: sure. with a proxy-first setup you typically put your gateway in front that does auth and rate-limiting, then it forwards to Redwood's hosted endpoint or to your Dedicated cluster. Redwood's API accepts a customer_token header so you can propagate the org ID. For billing and per-token attribution we can pass metadata (like tenant-id) as part of request headers. you still get per-token usage in the Console and via our usage webhooks.

[01:40] Marco Ruiz: are there any caveats around batching when we front with a gateway? we rely on batching to reduce token costs.

[01:50] Diego Alvarez: good question — batching is controlled at the runtime. if the gateway simply forwards synchronous requests, Redwood can still batch across inbound requests, but you want to avoid a gateway that does one request per connection in a way that prevents pooling. for consistent batching you can leave keep-alive on, and if you route by tenant we can configure batching windows or favor latency-first queues for certain tenants.

[02:22] Evelyn Park: and how does this interact with LangChain and LlamaIndex? our agent uses LangChain chains calling multiple prompts and storing state in an index.

[02:35] Maya Chen: we have small adapter examples — the SDK has a LangChain shim and a LlamaIndex connector. when agents hit the model repeatedly and use KV cache, Redwood's runtime exposes a KV cache eviction policy and per-request flags to bypass cache when you need deterministic fresh outputs. note: sometimes Kafka/redis key names get mis-typed in our docs as K V cash, so apologies if you saw that.

[03:02] Priya Desai: we saw references to a "sidecar" pattern where each service runs a small agent that handles token management and caching. pros/cons?

[03:13] Diego Alvarez: sidecar reduces tail latency because the cache is local and you can co-locate batching decisions. the downside is operational complexity — you need to ship the sidecar image, manage versions, and replicate metrics back to a central place. gateway centralizes ops but may add a few ms. given Orchid's partner-facing SLA, sidecar is attractive for low-latency endpoints, gateway is fine for batched back-office inference.

[03:45] Liam O'Connor: security question — if we go Dedicated or Private, how does KMS/HSM integration and audit logging work? we have encryption at rest and in transit requirements, plus SSO via SAML.

[03:58] Maya Chen: for Dedicated we offer customer-dedicated GPU pools with optional VPC peering. KMS integrations are supported — you can provide customer-managed keys; we support common providers and HSM via a connector. audit logs and full request traces are available for Private and Dedicated; hosted can provide extended logs as an add-on. SAML SSO and RBAC are supported for Console access. we'll send SOC2 docs.

[04:25] Marco Ruiz: another ops thing — how do you handle rate limits vs quotas? we want bursty traffic for devs but strict monthly quotas for partners.

[04:36] Jordan Patel: Redwood supports per-token rate limits (rps and concurrency) plus quota windows. You can configure soft burst tokens to allow short spikes, then throttle back. For partners we suggest per-route quotas enforced at the gateway level with a secondary guard in Redwood — that way you get immediate rejection at the gateway and accurate usage accounting in Redwood.

[04:58] Priya Desai: about observability — can we get per-request trace IDs so our APM ties model calls to end-user requests? we use Datadog and OpenTelemetry.

[05:10] Diego Alvarez: yes, we emit trace headers and support OpenTelemetry spans. You can pass a traceparent header and Redwood will propagate it into our traces; we also return a request-id header in responses. Console shows per-request token breakdown, latency histograms, and a flamegraph for per-model token spend if you enable the extended observability package.

[05:38] Liam O'Connor: curious about cold-starts and warm pools for agents with long sequences — our agents sometimes do 8k context. how does Dedicated handle that?

[05:50] Maya Chen: Dedicated can pin models to warm pools and reserve memory for large KV caches. for 8k sequences you want quantized models tuned for long context; we also recommend configuring pre-warming and a high-memory GPU profile. pricing changes for pinned capacity, which Jordan will detail.

[06:15] Evelyn Park: what's the easiest path for us to do a short eval without changing infra?

[06:21] Jordan Patel: hosted quick eval — we can mint test keys scoped to a tenant header, you run your gateway forwarding requests to us, and we provide a dashboard and webhooks. if you like the numbers we can move to Dedicated with capacity sizing.

[06:35] Priya Desai: can we run LangChain chains end-to-end in hosted? or do you recommend dedicated for anything beyond toy workloads?

[06:45] Maya Chen: hosted is totally fine for early agent dev and low-to-medium throughput. for production-level throughput, especially with KV-heavy chains and low SLOs, Dedicated is recommended. Private is for strict data-residency or air-gapped requirements.

[07:00] Liam O'Connor: one more on billing attribution — if we route multiple tenants through a single gateway token, how do we map usage back to tenants?

[07:09] Diego Alvarez: you can include a tenant-id header. Redwood treats that as metadata for attribution; billing can be exported per-tenant via our usage APIs or webhooks. If you need enforcement, implement quotas at the gateway and send usage reports periodically; Redwood can do reconciliation.

[07:30] Evelyn Park: can Redwood enforce model rollouts and automatic fallback? sometimes a model degrades and we need a safety fallback.

[07:41] Maya Chen: yes — Rollouts support canary and A/B with automatic fallback. we also have a quality monitoring system that can watch a set of prompts and alert on regressions so you can trigger rollbacks.

[07:56] Priya Desai: do you support streaming for agent responses? some of our UIs rely on partial generation.

[08:05] Diego Alvarez: streaming is supported; we stream token deltas and also provide chunked or SSE. For gateways, keep-alive and proper header passthrough are important so you don't interrupt the stream.

[08:22] Liam O'Connor: can you share any example configs for envoy or kong to proxy to Redwood?

[08:30] Maya Chen: yes — we have example envoy configs in the repo I'll share. it's just a standard TLS upstream with header injection for tenant metadata and trace headers.

[08:45] Jordan Patel: (quick) Diego will run a bench sim — Maya will share the quickstart and envoys. we'll also send SOC2 and pricing.

[08:55] Priya Desai: thanks. for the bench sim what metrics will you need from our side?

[09:02] Diego Alvarez: sample RPS distribution, sequence length distribution, percent of calls that use KV cache, expected concurrency, and any latency SLOs (p50/p95). if you can drop a small dataset or representative prompts that's helpful.

[09:20] Liam O'Connor: our SLO is 200ms p95 for simple retrieval-augmented prompts and 800ms p95 for complex agent chains. will that be realistic?

[09:30] Maya Chen: for retrieval-augmented prompts 200ms p95 is feasible on Dedicated with co-located index, for complex chains 800ms p95 depends on external I/O. We can look at pipeline optimizations: prefetching, caching intermediate states, and using smaller model components for routine steps.

[09:56] Marco Ruiz: curious about request-level de-identification before leaving our VPC if we choose Private. is there tooling?

[10:06] Diego Alvarez: Private includes hooks to run pre-send scrubbing via a customer-controlled pipeline; you can run a lambda that strips PII before calling Redwood. for Hosted we can offer a transform step as an add-on but it's more straightforward in Private.

[10:26] Priya Desai: any gotchas with the SDKs? our devs prefer Python and Node.

[10:33] Maya Chen: SDKs are mature for Python and Node. some older docs referenced "LanceChain" instead of LangChain (typo), but examples include the LangChain LLM wrapper, the async generators for streaming, and a small LlamaIndex connector. authentication is via API key or mTLS for Private. Node SDK had a small breaking change in 2025-10 where stream events changed shape — we included a migration note in changelog.

[11:05] Evelyn Park: how are errors surfaced — e.g., rate limited responses within a chain causing cascade failures?

[11:12] Diego Alvarez: we return structured error codes, plus retry-after headers for rate limits. We recommend agent workflows implement per-step retries and fallbacks. Redwood can also return partial outputs where applicable.

[11:30] Liam O'Connor: will the console expose per-route cost estimates so product can see how much a particular feature costs?

[11:36] Jordan Patel: yes — Console has per-route/model cost breakdowns, and you can tag keys/routes. We also have token-level cost estimates and a forecast tool for monthly spend.

[11:50] Priya Desai: what's the expected timeline to go from eval to dedicated? we typically need a PO and legal review.

[11:59] Jordan Patel: typical folks move in 4–8 weeks: 1 week for eval, sizing + PO negotiation 2–4 weeks, legal/compliance cycles vary. Dedicated provisioning can take a few business days once contract's signed.

[12:15] Marco Ruiz: is there an SLA for Dedicated?

[12:20] Maya Chen: yes Dedicated has an uptime SLA and latency targets in the enterprise contract; we can share the SLA doc.

[12:32] Evelyn Park: can we do a small POC where some traffic goes to Hosted and critical paths use Dedicated?

[12:40] Diego Alvarez: hybrid routing is supported — smart routing can route based on route, tenant, or cost rules. fallback policies allow Hosted as a backup.

[12:55] Liam O'Connor: okay this is helpful — curious about the bench run. what's the format for results?

[13:03] Diego Alvarez: we'll provide latency distributions, token cost per model, concurrency observations, and a heatmap of batching efficiency. we'll also record traces for a few example requests.

[13:20] Priya Desai: do you have any limits on number of index lookups per request? some of our chains do many small retrievals per step.

[13:30] Maya Chen: no hard limit at the platform level, but latency will add up. we recommend batching retrievals or using a local index to reduce round trips. if you offload retrievals to a co-located vector DB, we can optimize the data path.

[13:50] Jordan Patel: quick recap — Jordan send pricing + SOC2, Maya send SDK examples and envoy config, Diego set up bench and template, Orchid to send traffic profile. Next call: technical deep dive after bench results.

[14:10] Liam O'Connor: thanks all — we should loop in legal for Dedicated once we have the pricing.

[14:18] Jordan Patel: will do, and I'll include our standard contract terms for review. thanks everyone.

Recording end.
